subsection: 8. Demographic and social change: the status of women and social change, 1949–1989

notes.b: The population fell through most of the 1950s and early 1960s, then grew from the late 1960s, with emigration playing a major part in each phase.
points: The population stood at about 2.96 million in 1951 and fell to about 2.82 million by 1961 (about, verify both figures).
Emigration was the main cause of the decline, with most leavers aged between 15 and 25 going to Britain.
The population began to rise in the 1960s as birth rates stayed high and net emigration fell.
Emigration fell in the early 1970s, when jobs created by the First Programme and EEC membership reduced the outflow.
Emigration returned on a large scale in the mid-1980s, when unemployment rose and the economy stalled (see the notes on Lynch, Haughey and FitzGerald).
The share of the population living in towns and cities grew through the period, with Dublin's suburbs expanding rapidly.
Marriage rates were high in the 1960s and early 1970s, and the average age at marriage was falling.
Birth rates fell from the late 1960s onwards as contraception became more widely used despite legal restrictions.
Family size declined through the 1970s and 1980s, reflecting changes in women's education and employment.

notes.h: The marriage bar and the Commission on the Status of Women
points: The civil service marriage bar, which forced women to resign on marriage, was removed in 1973 (verify exact date of its removal across the public service).
The Commission on the Status of Women was set up by the government in 1970 and reported in 1972, recommending equal pay, equal access to jobs and reform of family law.
The commission's report was a turning point in the public debate on women's rights and gave campaigners a set of official recommendations.
The Irish Women's Liberation Movement was founded in 1970 and campaigned for equal pay, contraception and the removal of the marriage bar.
In December 1971 a group of activists travelled to Belfast by train to buy contraceptives, which were then not available openly in the Republic; the action became known as the contraceptive train.
In McGee v Attorney General (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that a ban on importing contraceptives for personal use was unconstitutional, a decision that set a major precedent.
The Health (Family Planning) Act 1979 made contraceptives legally available, but only through pharmacies on prescription and to married couples (verify the restrictions).
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 required equal pay for men and women doing the same or broadly similar work, to be introduced in stages.
The Employment Equality Act 1977 banned discrimination in employment on grounds including sex and marital status.
The Employment Equality Agency was set up under the 1977 act to promote equality and to help people who had been discriminated against.
EEC directives on equal pay and equal treatment, adopted in 1975 and 1976, reinforced Irish legislation (see the notes on the impact of EEC membership).

notes.h: Women in politics and public life
points: Women's representation in the Dáil remained low through the 1970s and 1980s, with only a small number of women elected to each parliament.
Mary Robinson was elected to the Seanad in 1969 and remained a senator until 1989.
Women's organisations, including the National Women's Council, gained a larger role in public policy debates in the 1980s.

notes.b: Meehan was a campaigner for women's employment rights and the first chairperson of the Employment Equality Agency.
points: Sylvia Meehan was appointed as the first chairperson of the Employment Equality Agency after the 1977 act (verify appointment year and details).
Her role put her at the centre of the enforcement of the new equality laws, including case work for women who had been discriminated against.
Contemporaries saw her as an effective advocate for women's rights, though some employers and politicians resisted her work.
Historians see the Employment Equality Agency as one of the first state bodies to give legal rights to women in the workplace, and Meehan's leadership of it is regarded as central to its early work.

notes.b: Robinson was a lawyer and senator whose campaigns for law reform made her a leading voice for women's rights in the 1970s and 1980s.
points: Mary Robinson was a barrister and academic at Trinity College Dublin before entering the Seanad in 1969.
As a senator she introduced private member's bills on issues including contraception and the decriminalisation of homosexual acts, which were not passed in her time in the Seanad.
She was a prominent supporter of women's rights and worked on legal cases concerning family law and equality (verify specific cases).
Contemporaries saw her as a liberal reformer who pressed the Oireachtas to change the law; some conservative critics opposed her proposals as a threat to traditional family values.
Historians credit her with building the legal case for reform in the 1970s and 1980s, a record that later shaped her presidency from 1990.

notes.h: Assessment: the extent of social change
points: Achievements: the marriage bar was removed, equality laws were passed, and contraception was legalised in restricted form by 1979.
Limits: women remained under-represented in politics and in senior jobs, and the pay gap persisted in many occupations.
Contemporary view: conservative voices argued that the reforms threatened the family, while reformers saw them as overdue.
Later view: historians see the period as the start of the liberalisation that transformed Irish society in the 1990s, though the change was slower and more contested than in many neighbouring states.
